text: A robot arm with three or more rotary joints, such as the common six-axis industrial arm.
An optional part of a UR PolyScope program that runs once before the main program loop, used to put the robot and tools in a known state.
The rate at which a PWM square wave completes full ON/OFF cycles, measured in Hertz (Hz).
A technique using a polarizer on the light source and an analyzer on the camera lens oriented at 90 degrees to eliminate direct specular glare from reflective surfaces.
A non-linear adaptation of the Kalman filter that linearizes dynamic and measurement functions locally around the current state estimate using first-order Taylor series Jacobian matrices.
A system design pattern where a robot stays in exactly one state at a time, switching between defined states when specific sensor events or conditions occur.
A ros2_control plugin that reads joint states from and writes commands to a specific robot, real or simulated, so the controllers above it do not need to know the brand.
The difference (residual) between an actual sensor measurement and the measurement predicted by the system state model.
A ros2_control controller that accepts FollowJointTrajectory goals and moves a group of joints through timed waypoints.
A modern, high-performance container file format designed specifically for robotics telemetry and multimodal sensor logging in ros2 bag.
Yaskawa's ROS 2 driver, which runs on the robot controller as a MotoPlus application and connects to ROS 2 through a micro-ROS Agent on the PC.
A name prefix, such as /turtlesim1, added to a node's name and its relative topic names so that identical nodes can run side by side without conflicts.
Writing and testing a robot program on a computer in 3D simulation, so the real robot can keep working until the finished program is downloaded to it.
An optical lens aberration where magnification increases toward the periphery, pulling straight lines outward from the center.
Maintenance that is scheduled, timed, or based on an operating cycle.
ABB's strongly typed, multitasking procedural programming language used across IRC5 and OmniCore robot controllers.
A Linux kernel built or tuned (for example PREEMPT_RT or low-latency) so that time-critical tasks such as a 500 Hz robot control loop meet their deadlines.
A machine that senses its surroundings, decides what to do with a program, and acts on the world, such as a six-axis arm guided by a program on an assembly line.
The fixed interval at which a digital controller reads its sensor and updates its output, such as 100 ms in the Arduino PID Library by default.
The target value a controller tries to reach, such as a desired speed or position.
The taught robot pose from which a wrist-mounted camera takes its pictures.
Rodney Brooks's 1986 reactive control design, in which simple behaviors are stacked in layers and higher layers can suppress the outputs of lower ones while the lower layers keep running.
The ROS 2 library that keeps track of coordinate frames and the transforms between them over time.
The RAPID data type that describes a tool: whether the robot holds it, its TCP frame, and its load (mass, center of gravity and inertia).
The first industrial robot, developed by George Devol and Joseph Engelberger, which began handling hot die-cast parts at a General Motors plant in New Jersey in 1961.
Driving to a list of destinations in turn, optionally doing a task at each one.
How an industrial arm is built: joints, degrees of freedom, the work envelope, coordinate frames, the tool center point, and how a controller interpolates joint and straight-line moves.
Plan and execute arm motions with MoveIt 2 on ROS 2 Lyrical: URDF and SRDF, ros2_control mock hardware, move_group, OMPL and Pilz PTP/LIN, and a UR5e in RViz.
Core 2D image processing: color space conversion, histograms and contrast equalization, global, Otsu and adaptive thresholding, contours, moments, blobs, Canny edge detection, and template matching.
Lab: the UR Modbus TCP server and its general-purpose registers, packing handshake bits in URScript, and writing and reading registers from Python with pymodbus (stand-in server, no hardware).
